summary: Specifies the protocol that implements Realm Specific IP. It lets an RSIP host negotiate with a gateway and lease some of the gateway's addressing parameters so the host can reach the global network. It runs at the application layer using its own port. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: It is the set of words a kid uses to ask the front desk to borrow a real name tag for a while and give it back later.

questions: how does a host lease addresses from an rsip gateway
how is rsip different from nat
subtitle: How a host behind an address-sharing gateway asks it to lend out public addresses and ports, instead of having them translated.

tldr.problem: A NAT rewrites addresses and ports behind the host's back, so it breaks protocols that carry addresses in their payloads or need addresses left unmodified, and it needs application layer gateways.
tldr.mechanism: RSIP defines a client/server protocol in which a host registers with an RSIP gateway and then leases a public address, or an address plus ports, from it. The host puts those values in its packets and tunnels them to the gateway.
tldr.outcome: The host keeps end-to-end transparency without application layer gateways in the RSIP gateway, at the cost of changes to hosts and gateways. This is an Experimental protocol, and the IESG note says its costs and benefits should be weighed against other ways of relieving address shortage.

facts.label: Suggested UDP retry timing
facts.value: 12.5 ms initial, up to six retries

today: RFC 3103 is an Experimental protocol and, in the data given here, is neither obsoleted nor updated. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why Lease Instead of Translate
sections.content:
A NAT translates the addresses of packets leaving one routing realm into addresses from another realm, and it does so without the hosts knowing. The RFC points out two costs. Any protocol that carries IP addresses or port numbers in its payload, such as FTP, needs an application layer gateway. And a NAT does not work with protocols that need addresses and ports to stay unmodified between source and destination, such as some IPsec modes.

Realm Specific IP (RSIP) takes a different route. The RSIP gateway, which sits between the private and public realm, gives each RSIP host at least one address from the public realm, and perhaps other resources. The host then places those assigned values in its own packets. Hosts must be modified to do this, but application layer gateways are not required in the RSIP gateway.

This document covers only the protocol for assigning parameters. Requirements and applicability are left to the companion framework in RFC 3102, and end-to-end IPsec support to RFC 3104.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal NAT is like a receptionist who secretly changes your name on every letter. RSIP lets you ask for a real name to use yourself, so nobody has to fix things up behind your back.

sections.title: Hosts, Gateways and Tunnels
sections.content:
An RSIP host lives in the private realm. An RSIP gateway is a router on the boundary that owns one or more public addresses and manages public parameters for its hosts. It may also act as a NAT for hosts that do not speak RSIP. Each side runs an application program: the RSIP client on every host, and the RSIP server on every gateway.

When host X wants to reach a public host Y, it first negotiates resources with the gateway. The gateway records a mapping between X's private addressing and the assigned resources, called a binding, so it can forward inbound traffic from Y to X. Every binding has a lease time.

X then tunnels its packets to the gateway using the assigned public values. The gateway strips the outer header and routes the inner packet onto the public realm. Inbound packets that match the recorded fields are tunnelled back to the right host. The defined tunnel types are IP-IP, GRE and L2TP.

There are two flavors. RSA-IP gives each host its own public address. RSAP-IP gives a host an address, possibly shared with other hosts, plus some ports that are unique per address. Hosts and gateways MUST support RSAP-IP and MAY support RSA-IP.
sections.plainLanguage: You borrow a real address, then send your letters inside a bigger envelope addressed to the front desk. The desk opens the big envelope and mails the letter inside as if it came from the borrowed address.

sections.title: Registration, Leases and Flow Policy
sections.content:
An RSIP host is always in exactly one of three relationships with a gateway. Unregistered: the gateway does not know the host, and the only valid action is to ask to register. Registered: the host has a client ID and knows the gateway's flow policy, but holds no addresses or ports. Assigned: the host holds one or more bindings, and the gateway forwards globally addressed packets for it.

Registrations and bindings both have leases, given in seconds from the current time. When a binding is created or extended, the registration lease becomes the larger of its current value and the binding's, so a registration never expires while a binding is still valid.

The gateway may also enforce flow policy. Locally, macro-flow policy hands out an address (RSA-IP) or an address with ports (RSAP-IP), while micro-flow policy hands out exactly one port at a time, and works only with RSAP-IP. Remotely, the host may be required to name the remote address (macro), the remote address and port (micro), or nothing at all (no policy). The host MUST then use the granted parameters only with what it named.
sections.plainLanguage: First you sign in at the desk, then you borrow things, and every sign-in and every loan has a timer. The desk can also have rules about exactly who you are allowed to talk to with the borrowed things.

sections.title: Messages and Parameters
sections.content:
Every RSIP message starts with three fields: a one-byte version (currently 1), a one-byte message type and a two-byte overall length. Required parameters follow in a fixed order, then optional ones in any order. There is only one message per packet.

Parameters use a type-length-value layout: a one-byte type, a two-byte length and a value. Defined parameters include address, ports, lease time, client ID, bind ID, tunnel type, RSIP method, error, flow policy, indicator, message counter and vendor specific. A "don't care" value is written by setting the length to 1 and leaving out the value.

The main exchanges are:

  • REGISTER_REQUEST and REGISTER_RESPONSE: the gateway returns a client ID, a lease time and the flow policy. If no method is named, RSAP-IP is assumed, and if no tunnel type is named, IP-IP is assumed.
  • ASSIGN_REQUEST_RSA-IP and ASSIGN_REQUEST_RSAP-IP, with matching responses that carry a bind ID, lease time and tunnel type.
  • EXTEND_REQUEST and FREE_REQUEST to renew or release a binding by bind ID.
  • QUERY_REQUEST to ask whether an address or network is local or remote.
  • LISTEN_REQUEST to receive inbound traffic on a chosen address and port, which is not needed for RSA-IP.
  • DE-REGISTER_REQUEST, which revokes all of the host's bindings.

The gateway answers problems with ERROR_RESPONSE, which carries one error. Gateways may also send ERROR_RESPONSE, DE-REGISTER_RESPONSE and FREE_RESPONSE on their own to revoke things.
sections.plainLanguage: Every note starts with a little label saying what kind of note it is and how long it is, then lists the details in a set order, like a form with boxes.

sections.title: Transport, Retries and Recovery
sections.content:
RSIP is an application layer protocol with its own port. Gateways MUST support TCP and SHOULD support UDP. Hosts SHOULD support TCP but MAY use UDP instead or as well. The client picks one when it registers, and the pair may not switch for the life of that registration.

Over UDP, timeouts and retransmissions MUST occur, and message counters are required. The RFC recommends binary exponential backoff with an initial duration of 12.5 ms and at most six retries. A gateway answers a duplicate request by resending its last message, and starts a session at counter value 1. Messages the gateway sends unprompted use a counter of 0.

If a host reboots, the gateway still thinks it is registered and replies ALREADY_REGISTERED with the old client ID, which the host should de-register before starting over. If a gateway reboots, it answers every message but a registration request with REGISTER_FIRST, and the host should treat that as lost synchronization. The RFC suggests short leases of several minutes to limit long outages.
sections.plainLanguage: If nobody answers your question, you ask again, waiting a bit longer each time. If one side forgets everything, the other tells it to sign in again from the start.

sections.title: Security and Registrations
sections.content:
RSIP does not provide security by itself. Hiding a private address space may give the illusion of security or privacy, but real security needs proper security protocols and cryptography. A gateway should prevent hosts from causing denial of service by requesting large sets of resources.

RSIP messages are not authenticated here. Hosts can currently be identified only by their local IP address or, in some cases, MAC address, and the RFC calls authentication desirable, pointing to RFC 3102.

For IANA, the RSIP port number is 4555. Error codes, message types, tunnel types, methods and flow policies are registered, and further values need Specification Required allocation under RFC 2434. The IESG note at the top warns of significant host and gateway changes and of operational complexity, and says the costs and benefits should be weighed against other ways of relieving address shortage.
sections.plainLanguage: The desk lends you a name tag but does not check who you really are, so you still need a lock on your own door. The desk should also stop any one kid from borrowing all the tags.
